## What this course is
The foundations of statistics and machine learning: probability, estimation, regression, classification, decision making under uncertainty, model selection, and neural networks.

The term is in two parts. Weeks 1 through 7 are lectures and self-check labs, ending in an in-person midterm with no AI assistant. From week 8 the class flips: studio in the room, and the rest of your time is the project.


You will be graded on two dimensions, shown separately on every rubric: Understanding, 45\%, and Judgment, 55\%. Understanding means explaining what a computation or model does, interpreting its output in context, pointing at evidence of a defect, and predicting what changes when an assumption or choice changes. Judgment means stating the decision and who makes it, stating the cost of being wrong, comparing the chosen approach with a credible alternative, matching the claim to the evidence, and saying what would change the recommendation. A correct number by itself demonstrates neither. Fluency, speed, confidence, and polish are not scored.

Understanding is not scored from correct output alone. I will ask you to explain the work and to predict what happens if a choice changes. Judgment is not scored from how sure you sound. I will ask for the alternative you rejected, the tradeoff, and whether you would revise.

## Using AI in this course
You are expected to use AI assistants. Getting results from one is fine. What I will not do is take a take-home write-up, script, or report and mark how good it is. That file may have been written by an assistant, and then I would be grading the assistant. Self-check labs score a number, an interpretation, and a prediction under a changed condition. Everything else that counts is something I can still attach to you: the page your team hands me before you leave, the paper practical, the viva, and the defense.

The rules are short:

1. Use whatever tools you want. There is no approved list. The midterm practical is the exception: no AI assistant and no machine. That hour is how I check that you can apply the basic principles and concepts on your own.
2. Disclose what you used and for what, in a short appendix on submitted work. No penalty attaches to the disclosure. A team that used an assistant for everything and can defend all of it gets full marks.
3. You are responsible for everything you submit, including the parts you did not write. If you cannot explain it, that is on you.
4. Three assignments require you to use an assistant and then check its work. The code will often run and the numbers will often be right. What you check is whether the assumptions are stated, whether the claims follow from what was computed, and whether the analysis answers the decision it was asked to support. Show how you checked.

The course tutor is a version of an assistant configured for this course: it answers R questions directly, asks you a question back before explaining a concept, and refuses to answer "which model is better?" until you tell it what decision the model supports. Setup is ten minutes, once, in week 1.

## What you will be able to do by December

- Apply the basic principles of probability, estimation, regression, and classification to a new problem without an assistant.
- Choose and fit an appropriate model for a stated decision, in R, and say why that model and not a simpler or more complex one.
- State what being wrong costs, in both directions, and set thresholds and choose loss functions accordingly rather than by default.
- Quantify uncertainty and say what it means for the decision at hand, rather than reporting an interval and moving on.
- Diagnose a defective analysis from its output: name the defect, point at the evidence, and predict which way the corrected number moves.
- Establish where data came from and whether it is what it claims to be.
- Evaluate a fitted solution against an AI risk framework: who is affected, in which direction errors hurt, and whether the data and the model support the use you are putting them to.
- Defend an analytical choice under live questioning, and change your mind out loud when the questioning is right.

## How a week works

Weeks 1 through 6. Before class, about 90 minutes on that week's module: read the notes, work the material, and submit the self-check lab. The lab is a short notebook with three or four auto-graded exercises and one written question. Ask the tutor anything you got stuck on. In class the block is lecture and worked examples. There is no studio and no project yet.

Week 7 is the midterm. After the practical, remaining class time is the project launch.

Weeks 8 through 14. Outside class you work on the project. In class, one block.

- Live analysis, 25 minutes. I analyse a real, messy dataset on screen with an assistant open beside me, and I hit dead ends on purpose, because watching someone competent be wrong and recover is the part you cannot get from a tutor.
- Studio, 75 to 90 minutes. Your team gets a dataset and a problem, usually an analysis that is already wrong in a way that is not obvious. You work it with whatever tools you like while I move between teams and ask hard questions.
- Critique, 30 to 40 minutes. A team presents; the room takes the analytical choices apart. You will be on both sides of this.

After class. Your team adds one entry to its decision log: the decision, the alternative rejected, the evidence, and what would make you revisit the choice.

Attendance is not separately graded. There is no studio in weeks 1 through 7 or in week 15. The practical, the viva, and the defense happen only in class. Missing studio is expensive and cannot be made up by reading.

## Grading

| Component | Weight | Understanding | Judgment |
|-----------|-------:|-------------:|---------:|
| Self-check labs and AI critiques | 15 | 10 | 5 |
| Studio pages | 15 | 5 | 10 |
| Viva | 10 | 5 | 5 |
| Midterm practical | 20 | 15 | 5 |
| Project defense | 10 | 5 | 5 |
| Final project | 30 | 5 | 25 |
| Total | 100 | 45 | 55 |

The same 0--3 scale is used on every assignment.

Understanding. 3: accurate mechanism, interpretation in context, and a correct prediction if a condition changes. 2: correct explanation, incomplete or needing a prompt. 1: repeats steps or output without saying why they work. 0: wrong, contradicted by the evidence, or cannot explain the submitted work.

Judgment. 3: names the decision and the loss, compares alternatives, calibrates the claim, and responds to a challenge for a stated reason. 2: the choice is defensible, but alternatives or consequences are thin. 1: a preference without a comparison or a decision. 0: no decision, no rationale, or keeps defending a claim the evidence contradicts.

I use the same five questions throughout. 1. What did you do? 2. What does this number mean? 3. Why does it support your claim? 4. What reasonable alternative did you reject? 5. What evidence would make you change your decision? The first three are mostly understanding. The last two are mostly judgment. A polished answer to 1 that cannot reach 3 is not understanding. A sophisticated model with no answer to 4 is not judgment.

Self-check labs. Six notebooks, weeks 1 through 6. None in week 7. Due before class, no late credit, lowest two dropped across labs and AI critiques, no individual extensions. Each notebook has at least one predict-before-computing question and one interpretation question with units and context.

AI critiques. Three, in weeks 9, 11 and 13. Each requires the claim, the evidence against it, the corrected claim, and how the correction affects the decision.

Studio page. On each of the 7 studio weeks (8 through 14), one page before you leave, in this order: the decision; the finding; the evidence; the alternative you rejected; the strongest check that could have failed; what would change the decision.

Viva. Five minutes, one on one, weeks 9, 10, 11 or 12. Slot assigned at random and posted in week 8; it happens during studio. Two questions: one mechanism or counterfactual, one decision, loss, or threshold. Week 9 and week 12 students are scored against the same anchors. Slots are randomised because a week-12 viva comes with more studio practice than a week-9 one. Week 8 is an ungraded practice round: I viva a few volunteers in front of the room and score them out loud, then you practise on each other.

Practical. Week 7, 60 minutes, on paper. No AI assistant and no machine; notes and the textbook are fine. The hour tests whether you can apply the basic principles yourself: choose the model, compute, interpret the result in context, and say what it does to the decision. A correct number is not enough. Understanding is the mechanism, the interpretation, and a prediction if a condition changes. Judgment is the alternative you did not take and the consequence for the decision.

Defense. Eleven minutes per team, Wednesday 9 December, 7:30 to 10:15 pm. Slots posted in week 13, two minutes between teams. The team is scored on how the artifact holds up. Each of you gets two short questions, including about work you did not personally build: one explanation or counterfactual, and one alternative, loss, or revision.

Final project. Teams of 3 to 4, locked in week 8, after the midterm. Proposal due week 9 (a real decision, a stated loss, and a check on where the data came from). Mid-build in studio, week 11. Decision log and a five-minute video due week 14; you watch two assigned teams and name the weakest claim you saw. Artifact due week 15. I do not grade the artifact as a document. Every major choice in the decision log names the decision, the alternatives, the evidence, the uncertainty, the reason for the choice, and what would make you revisit it. A logistic regression that answers the decision beats a gradient-boosted ensemble that does not. Model sophistication, number of methods tried, and visual polish are not on the rubric. There are no peer evaluations and no contribution percentages.

Team work is evidence about the team's judgment. The practical, the viva, and the two directed defense questions are how I score your understanding and your individual judgment. If those conflict, for example a strong project and an unsuccessful viva, we have a second five-minute conversation. That is to resolve insufficient evidence, not to punish you.

If the team is not working, tell me by week 11. After that we can reduce your individual scope or reassign you. Waiting until the defense is too late. I will not ask the team to grade each other.

Scores of each component are normalized to be out of 100. Grades will be posted on [Canvas](https://canvas.gmu.edu). This course uses Mason's graduate regular scale: A\+, A, A\-, B\+, B, B\-, C, F. Cut-offs: 97 (A\+), 93 (A), 90 (A\-), 87 (B+), 82 (B), 79 (B\-), 70 (C). Below 70 is F.

## Computing
All work is in R. Install R and the Jupyter R kernel in week 1; the README is in the course folder.

## Policies

Late work. Self-check labs are not accepted late, because the next lecture uses them; the two dropped scores cover this. Project components lose credit per day late. Anything in the room (practical, vivas, defense) cannot be made up except through the process below.

Missing an in-class assessment. Tell me before it happens if you possibly can. There is a makeup version of the practical held back for exactly this. Vivas can be rescheduled. Do not simply not appear; that is the only version of this that becomes a real problem.

Accommodations. Students registered with [Disability Services](https://ds.gmu.edu/) should contact me in the first two weeks so we can arrange things properly rather than hastily. This matters more than usual here because 20\% of the grade is oral. Accommodations for oral assessment are routine and include extended time, questions supplied in advance, a written component in place of a spoken one, and a separate quieter room. Ask if you need them.

Academic integrity. Using AI is expected and disclosed, so the usual grey area does not arise. What remains prohibited is what has always been prohibited: submitting someone else's work as your own, fabricating data or results, and misrepresenting what you did. Inventing a number, a source, or an analysis you did not run is the serious offence in this course, and it is the one an assistant makes easiest.

Group work. Team projects are collaborative by design. Self-check labs are individual: work with anyone you like, but the submission must be yours and you will see the same ideas on the midterm.

Recordings. Vivas are audio-recorded if you consent. The recording is so that a score you disagree with is something we can both go back and listen to. If you decline, the viva still happens and I score it from notes; there is then no recording to review later. Only I have access. Files live on Canvas and I delete them after the grade-appeal window for the term closes.

Project presentations are a required five-minute video, submitted on Canvas. They are visible to me and to the two teams assigned to review yours, not to the rest of the class. If you do not submit the video, that component is missing. Copies are deleted after the grade-appeal window closes.

They cover academic standards, accommodations for students with disabilities, FERPA and the use of Mason email, and Title IX. That addendum is part of this syllabus. The AI rules in this document are course-specific and sit on top of the university academic standards; they do not replace them. I am a required reporter under the Title IX policy in that addendum. Confidential options are listed there.

## What to do in week 1
Install R and the Jupyter R kernel from the README in the course folder. Set up the course tutor (ten minutes). Read the oral-checkpoint rubric. Knowing what you will be asked in the viva (your slot is in week 9, 10, 11 or 12) changes how you work in studio. Start noticing datasets you have access to through work, research, or an organisation you are part of. The strongest projects use data the team had to negotiate for or assemble. The weakest use a clean file downloaded from a competition site. Teams form in week 8 and you will choose a dataset then; it is much easier if you start looking now.

## Two things worth saying plainly
The most uncomfortable part of this course is being asked "why?" and not having an answer, in a room, out loud, while people wait. That happens to everyone here, including me. The ungraded practice viva in week 8 is there so the first time is not the graded one.

You will encounter AI-produced work you do not initially understand. Your responsibility is to interrogate it before submitting and defending it. I would rather that happen here than at work.
